turn_text: In December, Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin stated that failure to provide aid could lead to U.S. troop deployments, including possibly in Ukraine. Do you agree with that assessment of where this conflict could go, especially since aid this year has not been passed? And do you think the U.S. should be putting troops in Ukraine?

I don't think U.S. should put troops in Ukraine. And constitutionally, we can't put troops in Ukraine unless it passes Congress. And right now, $60 billion worth of aid can't pass Congress. So I'm pretty sure putting U.S. troops on the ground can't pass Congress. Thank God that Lloyd Austin doesn't have the discretion to make that decision. I think one of the best votes I've cast so far was to object to the waiver that allowed him to become Secretary of Defense. I think he's been an absolutely horrible Secretary of Defense. So, you know, the aid currently does appear to be frozen in the House. I'm curious, do you foresee a coming for Ukraine coming out of the house anytime soon? I mean, if it were up to you, what would you be pushing on this?

Well, certainly I've introduced the Define the Mission Act in the House. Got a lot of good co-sponsors in the House. Senator Mike Lee carried the Senate companion to it. And this is a restatement of the vote that we had on the National Defense Authorization last July. I referenced that earlier in our conversation. We got 129 votes on that. And that was just limiting, limiting a little bit of funding that goes through NATO. and DOD. Well, there is a healthy difference of opinion among Republican elected officials. You've got Neocon, Nikki Haley. I'm a never Nikki person for that reason and some others. And she would, of course, be ready for lots of wars in lots of places. just like her fellow South Carolinian, Lindsey Graham. And if somebody like that were in office, they would go about it very differently than Donald Trump would go about it. And we have the benefit of knowing how Donald Trump would go about it, because he went about it. He was very successful in peacemaking as president. He created enough uncertainty in our adversaries and rivals around the world to act as a deterrent. same kind of mantra as Reagan, peace through strength, supported a much stronger, more focused military. turn_text: So you've also been active in debates about the government's surveillance authorities. What's the problem as you see it? And how do you think we should fix it?

Yeah, so the Patriot Act is probably the thing most people know is post 9-11. It basically said that the government's going to be able to spy on you, but don't worry, it's just to keep you safe. And a lot of people cautioned at the time, this is going to be abused. Frankly, it passed, I think, with 98 to one in the Senate and it passed with all but like 63 votes in the House. And so George Bush was president, but a lot of Democrats will say, oh, well, this was a Republican idea because it happened when George Bush was president. It was overwhelmingly bipartisan at the time. And there were Republicans and Democrats who objected in the House. I think actually more Democrats did object than Republicans. But I go back to Ron Paul, who was a member of the House at the time. He was one of the most vocal critics. He said, this is going to be used to spy against Americans. It will weaponize our government. And lo and behold, it has, just as he predicted it would. And frankly, just as our Founding Fathers would have predicted it would, that's why they had the separation of powers. The whole bill of rights was passed to be a limiting factor on what the federal government can do. And the fourth amendment is the one that says that you have an expectation of privacy. And the government's supposed to get a warrant or a subpoena to go after your information, not to spy on you. And a lot of people today are so used to how infringed their right to privacy is that they'll say, well, if you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear. Why are you so worried about this? And that's not what the Fourth Amendment says. It says you have a reasonable expectation of privacy. There's no asterisk beside it. And I think we have to defend our Constitution. And the right to privacy is core to the rights of American citizens. That the default setting is Yeah, don't hurt people don't take their stuff. And one of the ways that you're harmed is when people invade your privacy because it never stops there. They start using that invasion of privacy to limit speech or to limit your freedom to travel. You know, and we've seen that through most recently, COVID domestically. And we saw it in great measure in Canada as an example where people had their bank accounts frozen because they went to a trucker rally or something. Those same kinds of things, you know, in a different way, maybe are done here in the US. And let's go back to Edward Snowden, who kind of tried to blow the whistle on this. He didn't follow the right whistleblower laws. Part of where he went public with his information about the way the US government was spying on its own citizens is after the Director of National Intelligence clapper had testified before Congress and lied under oath to Congress and said, we don't do that. And Snowden said, oh, yes, you do. And here's all the other stuff you're doing. Now, the way he did that was irresponsible, was dangerous, and I think probably contributed to the compromise of some of our intelligence assets. So, you know, it's not a blank slate for Edward Snowden, but the reality is it shouldn't be a blank slate for our intelligence agencies either and shame on us if we don't limit their ability to spy on American citizens. Surely, at this point, we've learned from our mistakes.
